title: Tenant surge failsafe, richer telemetry, and guided rollout for mitigating hosted API 5xx/timeouts
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Summary: During recent customer escalations we observed tenant-driven request surges that caused transient 5xx responses and long tail timeouts in the hosted API. This ticket implements a multi-pronged mitigation: a tenant-level failsafe to protect shared runtime capacity, richer end-to-end telemetry for root-cause isolation, and a guided rollout pattern so fixes can be deployed safely under load.

Background: Multiple customers reported elevated 5xx rates (502/503) and heavy retry amplification when their clients retried aggressively. Previous patches reduced some amplification but did not provide a graceful, automated way to decouple a noisy tenant without manual intervention. We need an automated, observable mechanism that: (1) detects suspicious tenant surge patterns quickly, (2) throttles or isolates the tenant while preserving SLOs for others, (3) surfaces causal signals for on-call and engineering, and (4) allows incremental rollout of behavioral changes.

Reproduction steps observed in logs:
- Tenant A emitted a large burst of concurrent stream-start requests at 2025-02-06T02:13Z.
- Edge and proxy queues increased; backend inference workers reported high KV cache churn and delayed response tails.
- Client SDK retried with backoff jitter but many retries overlapped causing connection saturation on edge pools.
- Systems returned 502/504 and many requests timed out at the proxy layer.

Observed signals: high socket queue length on frontdoor, sudden spike in kv cache evictions, per-tenant token/sec metric > 10x baseline, burst of 502/504 in application logs, rising avg latency P95->P99.

Hypothesis: The combination of a sudden concurrent-open distribution and absence of tenant admission limits allowed in-flight requests to exceed safe concurrency for runtime shards. This triggered excessive KV cache churn, kernel scheduling contention, and proxy queueing that surfaced as 5xx/timeouts. Retries from client SDKs amplified the effect.

Planned fix components (this ticket will coordinate the work):
1) Tenant Surge Failsafe: implement a lightweight tenant admission controller at edge that maintains a sliding-window QPS/concurrency estimate per tenant and automatically moves a tenant into a "degraded" mode when thresholds are exceeded. Degraded mode options: soft-throttle (token-bucket), adaptive-shed (reject low-priority requests with 429 + Retry-After), and fast-fail path for critical customers configured as exceptions.

2) Retry Harmonization Shim: modify hosted SDK and edge proxy to emit standardized retry-hints (Retry-After and idempotency info) and to enforce client-recommended backoff guidance in the response headers. This will reduce blind retry overlap and help client-side clients moderate behavior.

3) Telemetry & Tracing Enhancements: add tenant-scoped end-to-end traces that link edge admission decisions, proxy queueing, backend kernel scheduling metrics, and KV cache eviction spikes. Introduce a tenant-surge alert with pre-configured playbook links and severity mapping.

4) Guided Rollout: expose the new failsafe behind a per-tenant feature flag and implement a canary percentage rollout (1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100%). Each step includes SLO gates (error rate, P99 latency, kv-eviction rate) and automatic rollback on breach.

Acceptance criteria:
- New admission controller deployed in canary and validated with synthetic burst tests without inducing platform-wide SLO violations.
- Telemetry flows provide a single-pane tenant timeline showing admission decisions and downstream KV evictions.
- SDK/proxy headers reduce retry overlap in end-to-end experiments (measured decrease in request duplication during bursts).
- On-call runbook updated and integrated into incident response.

Risks and trade-offs:
- Over-zealous shedding could impact legitimate customer workloads; mitigation: conservative default thresholds and opt-out exceptions for paying customers.
- Additional telemetry may increase cardinality/cost; mitigation: sampling and aggregation for long-term retention.

Rollout plan:
- Phase 0 (dev): unit tests + local simulation harness (this week).
- Phase 1 (canary): 1% traffic to canary edge region (runtime-1.22/canary) for 48h with synthetic bursts and monitor SLO gates.
- Phase 2 (staged): 10% for 24h, 50% for 6h. Automatic rollback on SLO breach.
- Phase 3: full rollout and documentation updates.

Communication plan:
- Notify affected customers via account leads when tenant is moved to degraded mode.
- Publish post-deployment notes on status.redwood.com and internal runbook updates.

updates: 2025-02-10: Ticket opened by Asha Patel after on-call escalation from CS. Initial triage and metrics snapshot attached.
2025-02-11: Added prototype admission controller pseudocode and spike plan. Liam O'Connor volunteered to lead the patch implementation.
2025-02-12: Telemetry schema draft reviewed with Observability team; agreed to add tenant_id and admission_decision as high-cardinality only for 1h windows then aggregate.
2025-02-13: Integration spike: ran synthetic burst in staging; observed KV eviction linkage. Adjusted shed thresholds downward by 30% to avoid false positives.
2025-02-15: PR #4281 created with admission controller implementation (edge-proxy). Added unit tests and e2e harness. Waiting for security review on header changes.
2025-02-16: Canary deployment scheduled for 2025-02-18 02:00Z. On-call rotation and rollback playbook assigned to SRE team.
2025-02-18: Canary started; early telemetry shows 1.2% reduction in duplicate retries for synthetic workload. Monitoring dashboards updated.
postmortem_actions: Ship tenant admission controller with conservative thresholds and feature flag per tenant.
Standardize Retry-After and idempotency headers across SDKs and edge responses.
Add tenant-level synthetic canaries for key customers to detect regressions early.
Update incident runbook and CS notification flow to include automatic tenant flagging and contact steps.
Schedule follow-up audit in 30 days to evaluate false-positive degradation and adjust thresholds.
